articles.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
articles.summary: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights

top_comments: It's worth noting that the only modification the model made to improve itself was to reduce the length of its reasoning traces to avoid hitting the token limit. This is basically the same as the result from the recent weight-space programming article (https://rikiyat.github.io/blog/weight-space-programming/), which found that even Astra wasn't able to improve the performance of a model without this kind of obvious flaw.

Didn't Google's "sleep" paper already show this?https://research.google/blog/the-sleep-framework-a-new-way-f... > During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) memory blocks and updates its numerical weights using self-generated practice examples.

I’m hoping someone can explain this to me. They say “no training”:> for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training> it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only risesBut this sounds a lot like training, and “submitting only what works”, while probably not gradient descent by definition, also seems kind of obvious when you’re optimizing something.

articles.summary: We promoted developers into architects without informing them

top_comments: Am I an outlier in that every SWE job I've had has expected you to push back on requirements and design the data model for tickets you are handed? Even when the org was large to have an architect, they just were just a figurehead and designed the original system, and ongoing decisions were made by the dev who picks up the ticket.From that perspective, engineers are still engineers, just without the hands-on-keyboard coding. If that's all your job was, hands-on-keyboard coding with no decision making, yeah you're cooked and need to reskill.

No one is getting promoted. The most likely future is that your job will pay less and will be less fun, as you're increasingly just a "liability sink" for decisions made by an LLM.Try that with photography, painting, or music: "AI music has promoted musicians to architects".

I strongly believe good software teams (very rare) require members to play many roles. Sometimes you're a PM, sometimes you're an architect, sometimes you're the systems engineer. Enough people have enough context on the bigger picture that it's stable and there's a shared vision.More often than not, one person does the majority of this, and does their best to break up the responsibilities. A good CTO does that at the top, and it flows down through the ranks depending on how big the org is. Perhaps it's just a CTO and 5 engineers, perhaps it's a CTO with 5 divisions, each with 10 groups, with many teams.Flatter structures of engaged members works best from what I've seen, but you need to have a critical mass of people not only willing to take initiative, but empowered by leadership.

top_comments: I think when people set out to create a chess playing computer they thought we’d end up with something that we could deeply understand at an intuitive level. Instead, when you look at the Stockfish evaluation of a position, you do get an “explanation” but it’s really just the aggregate of a bunch of calculations, which are themselves stacked on top of the “stochastic parrot” NNUE evaluator.This leaves us in a very unsatisfying position as creatures who want answers to “why” questions. Intuitive answers are incomplete, and complete answers are either fundamentally impossible or completely incomprehensible or both.Feynman said something similar with regards to magnetism, but I feel that understanding a chess position is an even better example. Magnetism depends on facts about the universe which at their most basic level “just are”, whereas even a complex chess position is theoretically entirely explainable.

I wonder he good we will be at not understanding anything to an ever increasing degree, with absolutely no hope of ever catching up. We will be super bad at absolutely everything within sciences and engineering and completely unable to contribute anything of substance, outside our own moods and quirks.Can humans be okay with that? Can we be happy cats?

top_comments: 2018 tour was my favorite. Standing in line getting tickets was fun and loved getting to see them from the mosh pit for two nights in a row. Just saw them with my wife in Nashville about a year ago too and that show was excellent (also loved seeing all of the Gen X/millennials that are parents now bringing their kids to the show).

Trent Reznor really wants his fans to get a high quality show out of the performance. The sound quality is always top notch and when there's a multimedia component, it's used to great effect. For example, alongside video footage with a mass surveillance theme, hidden cameras were pointed at sections of the audience and were streamed on stage. It was a delightful touch.

I attended Fragility 2.0, NIN + Soundgarden, Cold, Black & Infinite, and Peel It Back. Fragility 2.0 was probably my favorite, but they are always incredible. 20 foot tall LED screens that moved and pivoted (from overhead lighting to background screens) in 2000 was pretty mind blowing. The scrim at the opening was awesome as well. Every show has its own things, but coming in with zero expectations and getting that was such a treat.
